text.p: Banking analysts on Friday said the Swedish government might sell all or part of its stake in banking group Nordbanken to the Wallenberg investment vehicle, Investor AB.
"It is a simple and neat solution," one Stockholm analyst told Reuters.
Financial daily Dagens Industri reported sources on Friday saying that the state is expected to sell 20-25 percent of its 58 percent stake in Nordbanken to Investor.
The deal could pave the way for a merger between Nordbanken with a market capitalisation of 38.2 billion crowns ($5.55 billion) and S-E-Banken which is worth 36.1 billion crowns.
Wallenberg companies own 15 percent of S-E-Banken's capital and 16 percent of the voting shares.
Such a merger has been widely discussed in financial markets in the recent weeks but analysts have pointed to complicated ownership issues.
"If the banks just merge (as they currently stand), the state would get too large a stake and the Wallenberg's too small a part," Goran Kallebo at Matteus brokerage said.
If Investor bought part or all of the state's stake, the Wallenberg family would dominate the new bank and the government would get the cash it most likely wants.
But although the government has said it intends to sell its stake, the finance ministry on Friday denied that it was taking part in any negotiations regarding Nordbanken.
Dagens Industri said the government discussed a possible sale to Investor in December and negotiations over a merger of the two banks were expected to start in late February or March.
"Why would the state deny this if it intends to start negotiations next month?," said Fredrik Myren at HSBC James Capel. "It could have chosen not to comment."
Investor refrained from commenting on the article, saying it was company policy not to comment on speculation.
Although several analysts find the Investor solution neat, they are divided about on the truth of the article.
"(The article) seems kind of homemade, it provides one of several possible solutions to solve the ownership problem," Kallebo at Matteus said.
"Nordbanken could have a share redemption (instead) ... or the state could agree to sell its stake in small parts to investors," he suggested.
But Investor's chief executive officer (CEO) Claes Dahlback said in a December interview in Dagens Industri that Investor is an interested party in changes in Sweden's financial sector.
Investor has enough financial muscle to act.
"Investor has nearly no loans and could borrow 25 billion crowns to buy the entire state stake, giving the Wallenbergs about a third of the new (merged) bank," an analyst said.
"Then Investor could redeem shares for five billion crowns or so to boost the value of the new bank and to get money to invest in IT companies (which it has said it intends to do)."

The newspaper article fuelled speculation on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, lifting Nordbanken's share by as much as 14,50 crowns but with the share price settling back to be 8.50 crowns higher at 224 crowns at 1045 GMT.
S-E-Banken's shares were up two crowns at 70 crowns and Investor share was up one at 296 crowns.
